Spagat, Michael, Brennen Fagan, and Stijn Van Weezel. 2022. From Gaddis to Mars: The Decline of War Enters New Territory. Working Paper.

Sundberg, Ralph, Kristine Eck, and Joakim Kreutz. 2012. [Introducing the UCDP Non-State Conflict Dataset](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0022343311431598). Journal of Peace Research 49(2): 351-362.

8.   UCDP also includes a conflict with fewer than 25 deaths in a year when it has passed this threshold at least once. But they consider such a conflict to be inactive.

9.   Project Mars formally only includes interstate conflicts, but de facto includes intrastate and extrastate conflicts because it has a broader definition of what armed groups are considered states: conflicts in which combatants are fighting over governing a state they both claim authority over can still be included.

10.   Correlates of War labels these conflicts as intra-state if they happen within one state’s territory

11.   Sometimes, however, these terms are used interchangeably. This becomes a challenge for researchers trying to identify the specific human toll of a conflict.

12.   We discuss how deaths from terrorism are identified in [our article](https://ourworldindata.org/the-global-terrorism-database-how-do-researchers-measure-terrorism) on the Global Terrorism Database.

13.   While UCDP and PRIO cover the same deaths and partially the same conflicts, their different sources often lead to somewhat different estimates:

UCDP collects data on deaths for each individual conflict event, whereas PRIO uses less specific summary estimates.

UCDP also looks at non-state conflicts and one-sided violence, which PRIO does not. Yet, PRIO’s summary estimates may still partially include deaths from non-state conflicts or one-sided violence that are closely tied to the state-based conflicts it covers.

UCDP only includes an event if it can identify the perpetrator. Because PRIO does not look at events, its summary estimates may partially include deaths where a likely perpetrator was identified as likely, but not conclusively determined.

These differences explain why UCDP tends to report fewer deaths than PRIO.

The joint UCDP and PRIO report [Estimating Battle Deaths: A Challenging Exercise](https://www.pcr.uu.se/digitalAssets/666/c_666984-l_1-k_hsrp_est.battle_deaths_1.2.13.pdf) discusses this further.

15.   Richardson, Lewis Fry. 1960. Statistics of Deadly Quarrels. Boxwood Press.

16.   Sorokin, Pitirim. 1937. Social and cultural dynamics. Volume Three: Fluctuation of Social Relationships, War, and Revolution. American Book Company.

17.   The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation’s Global Burden of Disease also partially relies on UCDP to calculate its estimates of [deaths from conflict and terrorism](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/death-rates-from-conflict-and-terrorism-gbd?country=~AFG).

18.   Peter Brecke, who assembled the Conflict Catalog, himself emphasizes that both the conflicts and the deaths included are incomplete, particularly for the distant past and outside of Europe.

19.   Militarized Interstate Events has plans to share the source(s) for each of its events.

20.   For example, here are [deaths in state-based conflicts by region](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-region) and [deaths in state-based conflict by conflict type](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/deaths-in-state-based-conflicts-by-type).

# Deaths from Conventional Wars (1800–2011)

[![Image 6: World of Data 's photo](https://cdn.voronoiapp.com/public/avatars/6c6df598-90f1-70d1-f773-cf1c1518e598_20241016235141.webp)](https://www.voronoiapp.com/author/OWiDCharts)

![Image 7: Deaths from Conventional Wars (1800–2011)](https://www.voronoiapp.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.voronoiapp.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fvoronoi-Deaths-from-Conventional-Wars-18002011-20240530153109.webp&w=3840&q=85)

There are very large differences in how deadly different wars are: most death tolls are relatively small, a few are large, and very few are extremely large.

The chart shows this for all conventional wars between 1800 and 2011, relying on data from Project Mars. Even though most wars killed several thousand people, we can barely make them out in the chart.

This is because the big wars were _much_ more deadly: wars like the Russian Civil War and the Korean War killed several hundred thousand people. And wars such as the Chinese Civil War and the Vietnam War killed between 1 and 2 million combatants.

But the deaths in the World Wars loom even over them: in World War I, more than 7 million soldiers died.

And in World War II alone, more than 21 million.

# Deaths from Conventional Wars (1800–2011)

[![Image 6: World of Data 's photo](https://cdn.voronoiapp.com/public/avatars/6c6df598-90f1-70d1-f773-cf1c1518e598_20241016235141.webp)](https://www.voronoiapp.com/author/OWiDCharts)

[@OWiDCharts](https://www.voronoiapp.com/author/OWiDCharts)

Follow

![Image 7: Deaths from Conventional Wars (1800–2011)](https://www.voronoiapp.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.voronoiapp.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fvoronoi-Deaths-from-Conventional-Wars-18002011-20240530153109.webp&w=3840&q=85)

There are very large differences in how deadly different wars are: most death tolls are relatively small, a few are large, and very few are extremely large.

The chart shows this for all conventional wars between 1800 and 2011, relying on data from Project Mars. Even though most wars killed several thousand people, we can barely make them out in the chart.

This is because the big wars were _much_ more deadly: wars like the Russian Civil War and the Korean War killed several hundred thousand people. And wars such as the Chinese Civil War and the Vietnam War killed between 1 and 2 million combatants.

But the deaths in the World Wars loom even over them: in World War I, more than 7 million soldiers died.

And in World War II alone, more than 21 million.

This **list of wars by death toll** includes some deaths directly or indirectly caused by the deadliest [wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War "War") in history. These numbers encompass the deaths of [military personnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_personnel "Military personnel") resulting directly from battles or other wartime actions, as well as wartime or war-related civilian deaths, often caused by war-induced [epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemic "Epidemic"), [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine"), or [genocides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide"). Due to incomplete records, unreliable censuses or contemporary accounts, differing counting methods, the [destruction of evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampering_with_evidence "Tampering with evidence"), and various other factors, the death tolls of wars are often uncertain and highly debated. For this reason, the death tolls in this article typically provide a range of estimates.

Compiling such a list is further complicated by the challenge of defining a war. Not every violent conflict constitutes a war; for instance, [mass killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") and genocides occurring outside of wartime are excluded, as they are not necessarily wars in themselves. This list broadly defines war as an extended conflict between two or more armed political groups. Consequently, it excludes mass death events, such as [human sacrifices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sacrifice "Human sacrifice"), [ethnic cleansing operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing "Ethnic cleansing"), and acts of [state terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_terrorism "State terrorism") or [political repression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_repression "Political repression") during [peacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace") or in contexts unrelated to war.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_by_death_toll#cite_note-1)

Averaging the death ranges, the total for the wars listed is about 570 million, of them 58 million for 500 BCE – CE 500, 117 million for AD 500 – 1700, and 396 million for 1700 – 2023.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_by_death_toll#cite_note-2)

This **list of wars by death toll** includes some deaths directly or indirectly caused by the deadliest [wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War "War") in history. These numbers encompass the deaths of [military personnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_personnel "Military personnel") resulting directly from battles or other wartime actions, as well as wartime or war-related civilian deaths, often caused by war-induced [epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemic "Epidemic"), [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine"), or [genocides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide"). Due to incomplete records, unreliable censuses or contemporary accounts, differing counting methods, the [destruction of evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampering_with_evidence "Tampering with evidence"), and various other factors, the death tolls of wars are often uncertain and highly debated. For this reason, the death tolls in this article typically provide a range of estimates.

Compiling such a list is further complicated by the challenge of defining a war. Not every violent conflict constitutes a war; for instance, [mass killings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_killing "Mass killing") and genocides occurring outside of wartime are excluded, as they are not necessarily wars in themselves. This list broadly defines war as an extended conflict between two or more armed political groups. Consequently, it excludes mass death events, such as [human sacrifices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sacrifice "Human sacrifice"), [ethnic cleansing operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing "Ethnic cleansing"), and acts of [state terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_terrorism "State terrorism") or [political repression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_repression "Political repression") during [peacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace") or in contexts unrelated to war.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_by_death_toll#cite_note-1)

Averaging the death ranges, the total for the wars listed is about 570 million, of them 58 million for 500 BCE – CE 500, 117 million for AD 500 – 1700, and 396 million for 1700 – 2023.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_by_death_toll#cite_note-2)
